articles.title: Support networks aim to help kids through the polycrisis
articles.summary: Sometime in the late 2000s, Pim Sullivan-Tailyour was sitting in the back of a car, headed toward her great-grandmother’s tiny town in the south of Thailand. She watched big mountains pass by out the window. She was just six years old but was about to be hit by an adult-size realization. “They were
articles._body: Sometime in the late 2000s, Pim Sullivan-Tailyour was sitting in the back of a car, headed toward her great-grandmother’s tiny town in the south of Thailand. She watched big mountains pass by out the window. She was just six years old but was about to be hit by an adult-size realization. “They were just quarried out,” she says. “Like half the mountain just dug out and disappeared, and so there was just this huge orange face.”  Although she probably didn’t know the word “quarry” back then, she sensed that what she was seeing was unnatural. She also knew, from family stories, that her mother had bathed in a nearby river when she was young, its water so glass-clear she could see fish swimming by. But the extraction had muddied the water. “We’re changing things,” Sullivan-Tailyour thought. “And it doesn’t seem right.” It was the first time it occurred to her that humans could alter the world—and that they were. For the worse.  She carried that knowledge with her as she got older and her family moved to the UK. There, she joined teenagers from other schools in the Schools Sustainability Network, an umbrella organization for groups that work on environmental initiatives.  But even with those connections, Sullivan-Tailyour didn’t encounter anyone at her own school who was interested in environmental activism. She felt lonely in her desire to push for change—and burnt out on working solo. “I was pretty much the only person who wanted to do these things,” she says.  That was when she heard about another initiative, called Force of Nature. A UK-based organization, in 2021 it had spun up Becoming a Force of Nature, a kind of informal online group therapy program, for kids and young adults worried about climate. The sessions aimed to help young people like Sullivan-Tailyour take their worries and turn them into action, stemming the exact kind of anxiety and burnout she was feeling. She signed up and soon logged into Zoom for her first session. Dozens of faces from dozens of countries looked back at her. “I realized that I wasn’t alone,” she says.  She began to suspect that kids at her school actually did feel the way she did, even if they weren’t doing anything about it.  Sullivan-Tailyour was right, it turns out: Global surveys have found that most kids are anxious about the state of the world—and not just about whether sea levels and carbon counts will continue to rise. They are growing up in a time of what some historians, policymakers, and economists are calling a “polycrisis”: The planet is warming, yes, but also a pandemic happened and could happen again, conflicts keep erupting, nuclear weapons lurk menacingly in silos, housing is growing impossibly expensive, groceries and gas can feel like luxury purchases, health-care costs are skyrocketing, authoritarianism is on the rise, partisanship splits populations, jobs are hard to get and there’s rampant worry AI will take more and more of them, and pings about all those things (and more!) arrive 24-7 in polarizing digital echo chambers.  That’s a lot. And it’s why online networks like Force of Nature have popped up. Although they’re not taking over the planet, they have gained thousands of participants. And they’re now dealing with climate not as an isolated issue but as one facet of a generally troubled world. The goal is to help young people, who are experiencing symptoms of depression and anxiety at higher rates than earlier generations, deal with their feelings about the multivariately changing future they are maturing into.  But the science on the effectiveness of these sorts of networks is still nascent, and psychological scholars—and some practitioners—say it’s time for the field to measure itself. That way, schools, parents, and kids themselves can know which programs to invest their time and resources in to actually help young people feel better.  Tough times The existential dread that comes with the climate crisis is so pervasive that it’s had an official name for many years: eco-anxiety. “The American Psychological Association calls it a ‘chronic fear of environmental doom,’” says Liza Jachens, a psychologist and assistant professor at the University of Nottingham’s school of medicine. “What people describe is closer to grief. A real sense of loss—not just fear of what is coming but mourning for what has already gone.”  Lise Van Susteren, a psychiatrist and coauthor of “The Psychological Effects of Global Warming on the United States,” a 2012 report for the National Wildlife Federation, has called it “pre-traumatic” stress; she sees it as a kind of anticipatory trauma. In a 2021 study measuring climate anxiety, 56% of 10,000 children and young people in 10 countries agreed with the statement “Humanity is doomed.” But there isn’t really a word to describe feelings people have about <waves hands> the rest of what’s going on in the world. A 2025 study from Polish researchers attempted to define “polycrisis syndrome” in the young people bubbling into adulthood in this hot soup of ingredients. The researchers assessed their reactions to the many crises using established scales of emotional and mental symptoms—things like the “Flourishing Index” and the “Difficulties in Emotional Regulation Scale.” “Most young individuals in our study face psychological challenges,” the authors write. In fact, more than 60% reported problems —difficulty regulating emotion, symptoms of depression, and lower overall mental and physical well-being—that they attributed to the cumulative stress of world affairs. That finding meshes with earlier, more climate-specific research suggesting that the kids are (sorry) not all right. In 2021, researchers published a landmark study in The Lancet Planetary Health measuring climate anxiety in 10,000 children and young people in 10 countries. articles.title: NASA calls off mission to rescue Swift gamma-ray observatory
articles.summary: Without a rescue, NASA's Swift Observatory is expected to reenter the atmosphere later this year.
articles._body: NASA and Katalyst Space Technologies announced Wednesday they are giving up on a robotic mission to rescue the Swift gamma-ray telescope before it falls out of orbit. The rescue satellite, named Link, launched July 3 on a journey to fly up to NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, capture it with three robotic arms, and boost its orbit high enough to escape a looming reentry. Link is about the size of a refrigerator, with two power-generating solar arrays and three xenon-fueled electric thrusters to send Swift into a safer, higher orbit. Katalyst, the startup leading the Swift rescue effort, said Wednesday that "ongoing attitude control issues" will prevent the Link satellite from completing its rescue mission. The spacecraft is still alive, and Katalyst said it will make the most of Link's remaining capacity, which may still allow it to get near enough to Swift for a demonstration of the satellite's close-in navigation system. articles.summary: US residents face trade-offs as delivery drone services such as Prime Air expand.
articles._body: Amazon wants to grow its Prime Air delivery drone service sixfold to reach nearly 500 cities and towns across the United States by the end of 2026. The planned expansions from Amazon and its rivals could make the convenience of delivery drone services available to tens of millions more people in the coming months—but will also test more communities’ tolerance for increased noise from daily drone flights. On August 19, Amazon announced it would soon launch Prime Air in the metropolitan areas of Chicago; Cleveland; Atlanta; Syracuse, New York; and Boise, Idaho, with more to come later in the year. Each Prime Air site offers delivery drone service within an area of about 175 square miles, with delivery times ranging from half an hour to an hour. Prime Air already operates out of Amazon warehouses in 10 cities across seven states. Those include primarily suburban neighborhoods of Phoenix; Tampa; Kansas City; Omaha, Nebraska; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Detroit; Houston; and San Antonio, Dallas, and Waco, Texas. articles.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all The AI industry’s boldest promise right now is that AI will soon improve itself, w
articles._body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all The AI industry’s boldest promise right now is that AI will soon improve itself, with almost no need for human oversight. But a new study suggests it might take a while to get there. Researchers found that AI agents still can’t conduct open-ended AI research—free-form investigations with no clear-cut answers that require the judgment and creativity needed to make genuine breakthroughs. The big question now is how crucial open-ended research is to recursive self-improvement—and whether AI systems can grind their way there without it, simply by improving on narrower tasks. Find out why the results may temper claims that recursive self-improvement is on the horizon . —Michelle Kim MIT Technology Review Narrated: what’s behind this summer’s heat, and why 2027 could be worse This summer has been a scorcher for much of the Northern Hemisphere. June and July marked the hottest two-month stretch in Europe since record-keeping began, the contiguous US endured its hottest month on record in July, and South Korea saw its highest-ever recorded temperature.   Climate change makes heat waves more likely and more intense. But there’s another factor at play: El Niño, which is already ramping up and is expected to have a bigger effect on global temperatures next year. Here’s what’s behind this summer’s extreme heat—and why 2027 could be even hotter . This is our latest story to be turned into an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 OpenAI has paused some model work over safety concerns It says its Astra model reached a “critical” risk threshold. ( Guardian ) + The slowdown sets it apart from Anthropic’s approach. ( Axios ) + OpenAI has made security updates after the Hugging Face hack. ( Verge ) + It’s also introduced a version of ChatGPT for teenagers. ( AP News ) 2 Chinese humanoid maker Unitree surged 629% in its stock market debut The IPO has underscored China’s lead in humanoid robots. ( Bloomberg $) + Unitree has become a key player in the Sino-US tech war. ( Reuters $) + It’s the world’s biggest humanoid firm and is already profitable. ( BBC ) + There’s hidden human labor behind humanoids. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 China is allowing Nvidia’s H200 chips into the mainland ByteDance and Tencent each recently received about 10,000 processors. ( FT $) + A new Chinese AI model could help defenders and hackers alike. ( Wired $) 4 5 Flock’s new AI tool lets police identify drivers by their movements It goes much further than tracking license plates. ( Wired $) + Here’s what Flock’s defenders are missing. ( MIT Technology Review ) 6 Prosecutors argue Meta deliberately hooked children on Facebook and Instagram The claim was made on the first day of a landmark trial. ( BBC ) + A scientist is building a missing map of childhood. ( MIT Technology Review ) 7 Even ICE has ethical issues with Meta’s smart glasses It’s banned them from the workplace over privacy concerns. ( NYT $) + Anduril and Meta are building smart glasses for warfare. ( 404 Media ) 9 A physicist proposes that the universe may repeat itself forever The same galaxies, lives and events could recur endlessly. ( New Scientist $) 10 A blind Egyptian developer has built an AI app that helps others “see” It uses cameras to answer questions about users’ surroundings. ( Reuters $) Quote of the day “ Arizona is Arizone. Illinois starts with a V. I mean, it’s crazy.” —Stacey Morris, a Kentucky mom whose son brought home a packet of AI-generated educational materials, tells local station WDRB about some of the errors. One More Thing The astonishing embryo models of Jacob Hanna When the Palestinian stem-cell scientist Jacob Hanna was stopped while entering the US last May, he knew the routine. Anything to declare? Any biological samples? But this time the agents’ questions touched on a specific new topic: embryos. Hanna didn’t have any specimens, but if he had, it would have been surprisingly hard to say what they were. That’s because he specializes in creating synthetic embryo models, structures that resemble real embryos but don’t involve sperm, eggs, or fertilization. They could provide unprecedented views of the earliest stages of human development, while also creating a new way to produce cells for transplant medicine. But as these models become more realistic, they are raising difficult questions about how far the science should go. Take a closer look at Hanna’s astounding embryo models—and where they could lead . — Antonio Regalado We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. Drop me a line .) + Take a guided virtual tour through Spain’s astonishing cave paintings . + Explore almost 2,000 prehistoric giants with the internet’s largest dinosaur database . + The humble convenience store has been lovingly reimagined as a floating public artwork . + If you’re looking to reflect on life or create a personal time capsule, you can write an email to your future self at FutureMe .

articles.title: From Undrafted to Unstoppable: The Story of Sydney Taylor
articles.summary: Every season in the WNBA, there always seems to be a player who shocks the world with a breakout game and even a breakout season. This year, that player is an undrafted rookie: Sydney Taylor.  Not only has Sydney Taylor taken the league by storm by breaking rookie records and leading the Chicago
articles._body: Every season in the WNBA, there always seems to be a player who shocks the world with a breakout game and even a breakout season. This year, that player is an undrafted rookie: Sydney Taylor. Not only has Sydney Taylor taken the league by storm by breaking rookie records and leading the Chicago Sky in the midst of an injury-filled season, but she has also made a name for herself in the W, proving that she can compete and dominate with some of the best in the league despite going undrafted. Taylor’s Journey to the W Taylor’s story about her road to achieving such a crucial role for the Sky is one of the most unique and impressive progressions that the league has seen, and it is only her rookie season. From 2019-23, Taylor spent four seasons competing for UMass, but it is not even that simple. In her freshman season, Taylor would play an average of 6.1 minutes per game, averaging just 1.9 points, 0.9 rebounds, and 0.5 assists per game. However, Taylor would make a momentous leap from her freshman season to her sophomore campaign as her stats multiplied, showing her incredible growth. Such progression is evident in her stats, averaging 15.6 points, 3.8 rebounds, 1.3 assists, and 1.2 steals per game in the 2020-21 season over 34.5 minutes of play per outing. This notable leap in Taylor’s ability to contribute for the UMass Minutemen on both ends of the court was evident as she continued to average approximately 16 points and at least four rebounds per game in her final two seasons. Because of the NCAA’s COVID-19 eligibility waiver, Taylor was granted one final year of college eligibility, where she would take her talents to Louisville after entering the transfer portal. Although her stats were not as padded and full as they were at UMass, Taylor remained a key contributor for the Cardinals as she put up 10.8 points, 2.8 rebounds, and 2.2 assists per contest, starting nearly every matchup for the Cards. Following her final season of college basketball, Taylor went undrafted. That said, her hard work did not stop there, as she began her professional career playing overseas. In the 2024-25 EuroBasket season, Taylor competed for Lithuania. Although her stats during her time overseas are not publicly available, Taylor’s dedication to her craft was once again put on full display when she made the move to suit up for Poland in the 2025-26 EuroBasket season. It was in that season that Taylor would put the world on notice, recording 22.7 points, 3.8 rebounds, 4.1 assists, and 1.5 steals per game in just under 29 minutes. Not only was Taylor able to score on a high level, but also efficiently, as she shot 56.7 percent from the field, 40.8 percent from three, and 79.4 percent from the free-throw line. This tremendous development and progress from Taylor in just one season was crucial to the next chapter of her life as she continued to work towards making it into the WNBA.   One Opportunity, One Turning Point On April 13, 2026, the entire trajectory of Taylor’s career would change with one offer. It was on this day that the Sky offered Taylor a training camp contract, an opportunity to show not just her skill, but also her potential in hopes that she could make the final roster. In the Sky’s second preseason game, Taylor showed up and showed out, recording 23 points on 7-of-13 shooting from the field. It was through this standout performance, as well as her incredible work ethic, that Chicago would sign Taylor to the official roster, a pivotal moment in her career. Since then, Taylor’s mindset has not changed in that she still strives to put forth her best effort. And because of that, she was able to put herself in the starting lineup just over a month into the regular season.   Stepping Up in the Sky’s Time of Need Heading into the 2026 WNBA season, it was without a doubt that Chicago was in the midst of serious adversity, with injuries as well as a completely new roster as the franchise continues to rebuild. The Sky began the season on a difficult note with Rickea Jackson almost immediately ruled out for the season with a torn ACL, DiJonai Carrington dealing with a lingering ankle injury that required surgery, as well as a few other day-to-day and week-to-week absences from Azur á Stevens and Skylar Diggins. Despite the discouragement that comes with these injuries, this challenging time for Chicago was also a time in which a star was born — or rather introduced. In just the fifth game of the season, Taylor put up a monstrous 27-point clinic against the Toronto Tempo on June 27. Although this standout performance from Taylor was not enough to get the Sky the win, it was certainly a spark of excitement for their future. Taylor has already recorded at least twenty points in six more games this season, and in two of those games, Taylor recorded her first two thirty-point outings in the W, highlighted by a career-high of 31 points against the New York Liberty on July 22. Not only did she beat her previous career-high of 30 points, but she also did so shooting 52.9 percent from the field and 57.1 percent from beyond the arc. Even though Chicago’s record does not completely display Taylor’s individual success, her growth, production, and impact on the team go far beyond the box score and have proven her value as an emerging star in the WNBA.   Taylor’s Latest Statement Coming off a strong team win against the Connecticut Sun just two days before their matchup with the defending champions Las Vegas Aces, the Sky were looking to keep the momentum going. Regardless of the fact that the odds were stacked against the Sky as major underdogs in this contest with the Aces, they battled until the final buzzer, with Taylor delivering a defining moment. Throughout this matchup with Las Vegas, Taylor was firing on all cylinders with no signs of stopping. articles.title: The X-Factor: Kaitlyn Chen’s meteoric rise
articles.summary: Kaitlyn Chen is currently putting the league on notice with the surprisingly successful Golden State Valkyries, but her road to doing so was anything but linear. Chen started her collegiate career at Princeton University, averaging 14.2 points, 3.9 assists, 3.5 rebounds, and 1.1 steals across thr
articles._body: Kaitlyn Chen is currently putting the league on notice with the surprisingly successful Golden State Valkyries, but her road to doing so was anything but linear. Chen started her collegiate career at Princeton University, averaging 14.2 points, 3.9 assists, 3.5 rebounds, and 1.1 steals across three seasons in the Ivy League (her freshman year was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic). The guard won three straight Ivy League Tournaments with Princeton and was named Most Outstanding Player of the Tournament in all three of those years, as well as winning first-team All-Ivy honors in 2023 and 2024 and being named the conference’s Player of the Year in 2023. Two factors gave Chen a tough choice to make: the Ivy League does not allow graduate students to participate in athletics, and Ivy League dominance doesn’t often translate to being drafted to the big leagues. Princeton’s hero ventured down the historically secure route, committing to play for Geno Auriemma on the UConn Huskies for her fifth and final year of college, filling a gaping hole at the point guard position left by Nika Mühl , who’d just been drafted to the Seattle Storm. Playing alongside stars Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, Chen’s role, of course, looked very different than it did in New Jersey, but the guard still managed to average 6.9 points, 3.4 assists, 1.8 rebounds, and 1.2 steals for the Huskies. Her resume at that point was good enough for Chen to be picked out of the stands in the 2025 WNBA Draft, joining a new Valkyries team that gave her the best chance at securing a roster spot. And secure a roster spot she did. Chen was initially waived by the Valkyries in May of 2025, but was re-signed a month later, achieving the rare feat of signing a WNBA contract as a third-rounder. The guard only averaged two points, a rebound, and an assist per game in 10.3 minutes coming off the bench, but the team overachieved greatly, sneaking into the playoffs as an eight-seed before being knocked out by the Minnesota Lynx.   A turning point in the narrative After serving under legendary coach Becky Hammon and winning back-to-back championships in Las Vegas, Natalie Nakase was named the head coach of the Valkyries, becoming the league’s first-ever Asian-American head coach in its then 29 years of operation. Nakase was outspoken about what this feat meant to her and her community, and has remained steadfast in preaching a message of inclusion. Chen is also a trailblazer for the Asian community, being the first player of Taiwanese descent to be drafted to and play in the WNBA. Having both Nakase and Chen repping for their respective communities was supposed to be something special, but some fans saw it differently. Suddenly, Nakase was accused of showing favoritism to Chen by not cutting her in the midst of her largely unimpressive rookie season. The chatter got even louder at the start of the 2026 season when, faced with a tough decision, Golden State had to cut fan-favorite Kate Martin to make room for Gabby Williams and 2025 draftee Justė Jocytė, who was joining the team for the first time after fulfilling her duties in Europe . Given Veronica Burton’s breakout Most Improved Player season in 2025, Chen and Martin, as guards, were naturally on the hot seat, and the choice to cut Martin struck a nerve with many. Chen’s heard the talk. During her appearance on Sue Bird’s “Bird’s Eye View” podcast, Chen spoke to the challenges of being put into a box because of her identity and how, especially during her rookie season, it was hard for her to feel like she was an individual instead of a tool for creating narratives about the W. Basketball has a way of drowning out all of the other noise around it, and now that Chen actually has the chance to play as much basketball as she can for the Bay, it’s clear that she was 100 percent deserving of the Valkyries’ last roster spot. In 14.8 minutes per game off the bench, Chen has averaged seven points and two assists, which may seem minimal, but her impact on the game is often very loud, especially in the minutes during which Burton and Williams cannot get anything going. Chen shoots 54.7 percent from the field and has dropped over 15 points four times this year as the Valkyries have coasted to being the third seed. Chen leads the bench unit alongside Janelle Salaün , who’s solidified herself as the 6th Player of the Year favorite by leading all reserves in points, rebounds, 3PM, PPG, and 20-point games. “We have to be the only team that has multiple 6POTY options,” said Gabby Williams after Chen scored 12 points in the third quarter to lead the Valkyries to a win against the Indiana Fever in July. “It’s insane.” Chen sports one of the league’s most impressive layup packages—especially given her shorter stature—and has a way of setting up isos that all but guarantee that she’ll score a quick and easy two points when Golden State needs it most. A player who was once being told she didn’t deserve to play in the W was now, just a year later, getting incredulous looks from opposing teams’ fans. Now, major national sports outlets see her as valuable enough to include in a trade for the likes of Kelsey Plum.   A building block for the future The sad reality of expansion is that there’s no current roster in the W that will look the same come 2028, and then 2030. The expansion draft will come along like the Grim Reaper yet again, stealing fan favorites and benched hidden gems and giving them the opportunity to shine in a new market and create new fans in new corners of the country. With a team as well-rounded as the Valkyries, especially, this is a devastating part of the game to come to terms with. Who knows how much longer Chen will get to rock the iconic lavender in front of Ballhalla, or how much longer she, along with Nakase, will be there to inspire young Asian girls in and around San Francisco. In the meantime, though, the Valkyries need to thank their lucky stars that they decided to take a c

articles.title: Who won the 2026 trade deadline?
articles.summary:
The 2026 WNBA trade deadline came and went—most teams decided to stick with the rosters they’ve had since May, while a few went out on a limb to make some moves to help with the playoff push as the season winds down. The new CBA and expansion teams have made this season one of the…

T
articles._body: The 2026 WNBA trade deadline came and went—most teams decided to stick with the rosters they’ve had since May, while a few went out on a limb to make some moves to help with the playoff push as the season winds down. The new CBA and expansion teams have made this season one of the most interesting in the league’s history, and the few trades we saw might make it more so. If you’re wondering what each of these moves means for the teams involved, here’s a breakdown:   Aneesah Morrow is headed north for…almost nothing? Toronto Tempo receive: Aneesah Morrow Connecticut Sun receive: Rights to Maria Kliundikova, 2028 second-round draft pick On July 31st, the Connecticut Sun sent 2025 No. 7 pick Aneesah Morrow to the Toronto Tempo in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and the rights to Maria Kliundikova. This trade came in the wake of a successful, yet confusing year for Morrow, who’s averaged 11.6 points, 8.9 rebounds, and 1.5 stocks (all career highs) in 20 games, all in the middle of inexplicably missing multiple outings for the Sun. Connecticut has a bit of a “too many cooks in the kitchen” problem in the frontcourt—on many other teams, Morrow would have easily been a starter playing significant, impactful minutes, but behind Brittney Griner and Olivia Nelson-Ododa, she wasn’t afforded the opportunity to do so. The Tempo, on the other hand, needed a big to round out an already skilled and capable roster. Marina Mabrey and Brittney Sykes are leading the ship from the backcourt, while Nyara Sabally and Izzy Harrison, who’s been killing it since she returned from injury in June, have bolstered the team’s production down low, but the 2026 expansion team was still in need of another dynamic scorer and strong post presence that can punish opposing teams below the basket and take over when the 3-ball isn’t falling, or even take a few shots from deep herself. Morrow is just that. I’m already imagining how different the Tempo vs. Valkyries season series could have looked if she was there earlier to give Sabally a few more minutes to rest on the bench or to draw Kiah Stokes out of the paint to allow Harrison to drive to the basket. Given the whispers that the Sun were allegedly in talks with the Liberty for Morrow, I struggle to believe that this was the best Connecticut could have gotten for her. Seriously, not even a first-round pick? Perhaps this is a bit of resistance from the Sun front office, who knows its days might be numbered as the team gears up to move down south, or maybe something happened behind the scenes, which could explain the plethora of “personal reason” DNPs. Maybe the Houston ownership team made it clear to Connecticut that Edwards and Nelson-Ododa were their bigs of the future, not Morrow. All I know is, I’m sure there are plenty of GMs kicking themselves for not trying to snag the young LSU alum before the deadline. Clearly they wouldn’t have had to give up much.   Kelsey Plum traded as time ticks down, LA somehow ends up victorious Phoenix Mercury receive: Kelsey Plum Los Angeles Sparks receive: Monique Akoa Makani, 2027 first-round draft pick, 2028 second-round draft pick Kelsey Plum easily generated the most noise as the trade deadline approached. The five-time All-Star guard has been tearing through the league, averaging 23.6 points, 6.2 assists, and 1.1 steals per game, although injuries have prevented her from staying in early MVP conversations. Plum is set to become a free agent after the 2026 WNBA season, and made it clear she was interested in moving on from Los Angeles, who’ve struggled to win despite impressive offensive production from Plum and Nneka Ogumike. In order to not end the Plum/LA saga empty-handed, the Sparks suddenly had to find a team that would be willing to give up young players and/or draft capital for an aging Plum that still planned to field offers during the offseason. Rumors spread, and much of the WNBA sphere was convinced we’d see Plum join the already highly-seeded Golden State Valkyries alongside All-Star Gabby Williams, giving the defensive team a much-needed go-to scorer. Given Natalie Nakase’s “everybody eats” philosophy, though, it was unlikely the Valkyries would be willing to part with one of its coveted bench players for a shot in the sweepstakes. Turns out, it was the Phoenix Mercury that were willing to take the chance; the 2025 runners-up dealt young guard Monique Akoa Makani, a 2027 first-round pick, and a 2028 second-round pick for Plum. So far, the on-court fit has looked good: mere hours after landing, Plum dropped 20 points and 6 assists in 21 minutes in her first game alongside Alyssa Thomas (who recorded a triple-double, in true AT fashion), DeWanna Bonner (who became the W’s winningest player with Phoenix’s win) and Kahleah Copper (who scored 31). The biggest question with this trade, however, was never whether Plum would fit in with the Mercury’s big three—because of course she can and most likely will—but rather what happens at the end of the season. The Mercury have had a tumultuous year, and these next 13 games will need to be played phenomenally to give the veteran-led team a chance at the playoffs. Even if they do sneak in as an eighth seed, does Plum truly push this team over the edge enough to beat the likes of the Minnesota Lynx, Las Vegas Aces, or even the Valkyries? More importantly, Plum has told the media that, wherever she ends this season, she will be a full participant in the 2027 free agency process. Essentially, the Mercury could have traded away a young player and a potential lottery pick for a 14-game rental from Plum: an extremely short-sighted and nonsensical move. In the long term, neither team won this trade. The Sparks gave up picks that have turned into All-Star and All-WNBA players on the road to acquire Plum in the first place, but failed so drastically to capitalize that the guard was practically buzzing to leave at the first opportunity to do so. articles.title: Winsidr‘26 Power Rankings — Volume 6
articles.summary: With the league back from the All-Star break, but only a couple of weeks away from the FIBA break, it’s crunch time for a lot of teams. While the bottom half of the standings is staying pretty consistent, things could get interesting up top before the regular season comes to a close. A couple of&
articles._body: With the league back from the All-Star break, but only a couple of weeks away from the FIBA break, it’s crunch time for a lot of teams. While the bottom half of the standings is staying pretty consistent, things could get interesting up top before the regular season comes to a close. A couple of teams came back from break looking fully rejuvenated, while others have plummeted. Here are a few teams we’ve seen leap, a couple who’ve been knocked down, and some surprising takeaways. Teams on the Rise Washington Mystics The Washington Mystics are quickly becoming the most threatening team in the league. They went into the All-Star break on a two-game winning streak against two tough opponents ‚ the Aces and the Valkyries. Seemingly, the confidence that came with those dubs did not disappear when the team returned from the break. They’ve now won seven games in a row — five against serious playoff opponents. Not only is this recent streak the longest active one in the W, but it’s also one away from their longest in franchise history. They’ve risen from spot No. 8 in our last volume to No. 6. The Mystics are firmly sitting in playoff contention now, but have two tough games ahead of them. They will face the Las Vegas Aces back-to-back this week. The key to them doing it again will be Shakira Austin, who is having the season of her life.   Minnesota Lynx In our last volume, the Lynx were sitting at No. 2 right under the Las Vegas Aces. Well, they’ve regained a tight hold on the top spot in the league. Just yesterday, they became the first team to officially clinch a playoff spot — but now they aim higher: the No. 1 seed. It’s looking like theirs to lose right now, as the Valkyries are three games back. Minnesota has won 12 of its last 13 games, beating opponents like Las Vegas, New York, Indiana, and Dallas. With the return of Napheesa Collier to the lineup, there’s no telling how much more damage this team could do before the regular season ends. Their other elite pieces have all been stepping up in the right ways, as well. Kayla McBride just set a new WNBA single-game record in 3-pointers made, with 10. She finished the night with a whopping 43 points. Rookie sensation Olivia Miles has been unstoppable, averaging 24.3 points per game over their last four. This squad isn’t just sitting pretty ‘on the rise’; they’re staring a deep playoff run right in the face.   Teams on the Decline Dallas Wings When we say a couple of teams have plummeted since the All-Star break, unfortunately, we’re talking about the Dallas Wings. Since returning, they’ve lost five of their last six games. They’ve developed some apparent cracks. Azzi Fudd, who has become an integral part of their starting lineup, has been out due to injury. Luckily, the Wings had a great first half of the season, so they could afford a bit of a slow start back into things. But it can’t go on for much longer. They’ve mostly been losing to other playoff teams, like Minnesota, Golden State, Washington and Atlanta. While earlier in the season, this probably wouldn’t have been cause for concern, it’s now becoming close to playoff time. These are the exact teams they’ll likely be facing in the postseason; getting some wins and confidence against them now could’ve been great for future meetings. This week, they’ll face off against Indiana and Golden State with hopes of getting their season back on track.   Toronto Tempo A few weeks ago, the Tempo’s playoff hopes were still in the conversation, but now, it’s not looking very likely. In our last volume, Toronto was sitting at No. 9. They’ve dropped to No. 13 this time around. They’ve lost their last eight games. While it’s been a pretty tough stretch, against opponents like Golden State, Minnesota and Vegas, they still needed to grab a few of those wins to keep their season alive. Injuries have hit the Tempo pretty hard this season. Brittney Sykes has been unavailable since mid-June. Kiki Rice just returned to play for the first time since early June. However, Toronto did add a key piece before the trade deadline. Aneesah Morrow was traded to the Tempo, rejoining her vet, Marina Mabrey. She brings a frontcourt presence this team desperately needed. Sykes is expected to return before the season ends. Maybe with the team fully healthy and a powerful new addition, they can make a push back up the standings.   Surprising Takeaways Bottom-Half Teams with Promising Pieces Speaking of trades, Kelsey Plum has joined the Phoenix Mercury. While it would take a lot of top-half movement for the Merc to squeeze into the playoffs, it’s still fun to watch this team — especially with KP in the backcourt. She, Alyssa Thomas and Kahleah Copper all have experience playing together for Team USA. That connection has shown itself in Plum’s early games with Phoenix. She put up 20 points, one rebound and four assists during her debut. Now, the question is: Does she stay in Phoenix for the 2027 season…? The Chicago Sky is another bottom-half team that saw a bit of a jump in our rankings. They hopped up three spots since our last volume. Rookie Sydney Taylor is their most promising and surprising piece. Before the season, I’m not sure anyone would’ve expected this undrafted rookie to hit a game-winning 3-pointer over the Las Vegas Aces — but here we are. If the Sky can stay healthy next season, she could be what takes this team far. The post Winsidr‘26 Power Rankings — Volume 6 appeared first on Winsidr .

articles.title: Where the Next Generation Begins: Inside Basketball Without Borders
articles.summary: While most of the buzz following the record-breaking WNBA All-Star weekend centered on the league’s biggest stars, one of the weekend’s most meaningful stories unfolded just a few miles away.  At the Advocate Center, just a few blocks from the United Center arena, 40 of the world’s top high-schoo
articles._body: While most of the buzz following the record-breaking WNBA All-Star weekend centered on the league’s biggest stars, one of the weekend’s most meaningful stories unfolded just a few miles away. At the Advocate Center, just a few blocks from the United Center arena, 40 of the world’s top high-school-aged prospects gathered for the fourth Women’s Basketball Without Borders (BWB) All-Star Camp.Over three days, they trained, competed, and learned from current and former players and industry professionals, getting a first look at what it takes to play at the highest level. For many of them, this wasn’t just another basketball camp. It was a chance to see how close or how far they are from the dream they’ve been chasing. There was a particular kind of feeling that settled over a gym full of young players who had no idea yet just how good they might become. It’s not exactly nerves or confidence. It’s something closer to possibility. That’s the feeling that filled the room that weekend at Basketball Without Borders, a program that, since 2001, has quietly become one of the most important development programs in the sport. More than 4,900 players from 149 countries and territories have passed through it. 27 campers from last year earned NCAA Division I scholarships. The list of former campers who have gone on to the WNBA continues to grow, including Dominique Malonga, Aaliyah Edwards, Kamilla Cardoso, Ezi Magbegor, and Jade Melbourne, to name a few. Walking through the gym, it wasn’t hard to imagine another future WNBA star among this year’s group. That’s the strange magic of BWB. You’re never just watching a camp; you’re watching the earliest chapter of their career. Photo credit: Audrey Yacou Over the weekend, campers rotated through skill development, athletic testing, 3-on-3 and 5-on-5 competition, but basketball was only part of the curriculum. More than just basketball, players also participated in life skills sessions, a reminder that the BWB program measures its success way beyond just the points totals. WNBA scouts and NCAA coaches watched from the sidelines, a quiet but undeniable signal that for some of the players, this gym is where the opportunity actually begins.   The French Wave Among the many stories unfolding inside the gym, one stood out in particular: the continued rise of French basketball, a trend that’s no longer a subplot in the WNBA international story, but close to a headline. Few countries have produced as much young WNBA talent in recent years as France. Between Dominique Malonga, Gabby Williams, Pauline Astier and a growing pipeline of young talent, France has established itself as one of the league’s strongest international contributors. And that success was not lost on the French prospects at BWB. Back at the camp, several French prospects were watching closely, not as distant fans but as players hoping to follow a similar path. Among them, Sarah Cissé. For Cissé, being selected to the camp was a goal and a tremendous opportunity to walk in the footsteps of players who came before her. “It was the reward of the hard work I put in during the year, and the experience has been rich on many levels, and the energy gave me more motivation for the future,” said Cissé. Watching Malonga dunk during the All-Star game wasn’t just entertainment for Cissé; it was motivation. “The WNBA does not feel as far away anymore. If you work hard and stay focused, you can get there,” said Cissé. “Seeing Dominique, who’s close to us in age, makes it feel possible”. Cissé also spoke about how valuable it was to compete alongside players from every corner of the world. Every practice brought a different style of play, a new challenge, and another opportunity to learn. That’s what makes Basketball Without Borders unique.   More than a camp Yes, the camp is about developing skills. But it’s also about exposing young players to different perspectives, different cultures and different ways of approaching the game. For three days, the gym turned into a classroom led by some of the game’s most experienced voices. Current Washington Mystics guard Georgia Amoore joined two-time WNBA Champion Tamecka Dixon, former Spain national team standout Anna Montañana , Meighan Simmons and Shanece Sims. Leading the camp and returning as camp director for the fourth year was WNBA legend and Boston Celtics Vice President of Team Operations and Organizational Growth Allison Feaster. For Feaster, BWB represents far more than just a weekend of drills and scrimmages. It’s an investment in the future of the game. “This camp is the beauty of the game in itself”, Feaster told Winsidr. “The league and the greater game prioritize being borderless. It’s important to invest in the next generation of international players because the game is global.” Feaster strongly believes that the continued growth of the WNBA depends on creating opportunities for young players around the world long before they reach the professional level. “We want players from all across the globe to be represented in the WNBA,” she said. “If we’re not focusing on these types of grassroots events, it’s hard for us to grow the game at the elite level.” Beyond developing future stars, Feaster sees BWB as a reflection of the basketball community as a whole, one where players, coaches and executives from different countries all play a role in growing the sport. Photo credit: Audrey Yacou Many players who left Chicago that weekend will continue their journeys in high school, college, or some in the professional league they are already playing in overseas. A few will likely hear their name called on WNBA Draft night next year for some, or years from now for others. And if history is any indication, one of the campers sharing the floor at BWB may one day return to All-Star Weekend, not as a spectator or camper, but as one of the stars inspiring the next generation. articles.title: The Roots of Megan DiLeo’s Growth and Success in Portland
articles.summary: The Portland Fire and Toronto Tempo were the two new expansion teams to debut this WNBA season. But, for Portland, WNBA basketball is not new to the city. The WNBA is back in Portland for the first time since 2002. Currently, the Fire sit with an 11-18 record. Despite the sub-.500 record and sitt
articles._body: The Portland Fire and Toronto Tempo were the two new expansion teams to debut this WNBA season. But, for Portland, WNBA basketball is not new to the city. The WNBA is back in Portland for the first time since 2002. Currently, the Fire sit with an 11-18 record. Despite the sub-.500 record and sitting in tenth place in the standings, the team is still in the mix for a postseason appearance, chasing after what would most likely be the final playoff spot as the eighth seed. The players have built up a lot of excitement for the future of the franchise. One of the faces of the second iteration of the Fire is Megan DiLeo (formerly Gustafson, after getting married a few weeks ago), who is currently averaging 12.6 points per game (PPG), 3.8 rebounds per game (RPG) and 0.9 assists per game (APG) for the team. She has also been a starter for 18 of the 29 games. DiLeo recently achieved an individual milestone; on July 11, she reached 1,000 career points in a road victory against the Atlanta Dream. GO MEGAN GO MEGAN Megan Gustafson has scored 1,000 career points. pic.twitter.com/mhzoYnX0ue — Portland Fire (@theportlandfire) July 11, 2026 It is a massive accomplishment for DiLeo, as she has been met with different challenges and stops thus far in her WNBA career, working to solidify herself as not just a long-term rotation player on a roster, but someone who can be among the most important players on a team. Yet, that role of being a very important and relied-upon player for a team is nothing new to her. Before the 2019 WNBA draft, DiLeo was a star at Iowa, especially in her senior season, which included a 1,000-point season, a trip to the Elite Eight of the NCAA tournament, and National Player of the Year honors. DiLeo had a decorated college career that culminated with her jersey number now hanging in the rafters of Carver-Hawkeye Arena. After playing at Iowa, she was drafted by the Dallas Wings in the second round of the 2019 draft. However, the success she enjoyed in college did not translate to the league right away. In her rookie season with the Wings, DiLeo averaged 2.9 PPG and 2.5 RPG in 25 games played. The following season, she averaged 1.6 PPG and 1.2 RPG in only nine games played. DiLeo eventually moved on and played for the Washington Mystics during the 2021 season. But, she appeared in only 11 games during her stint with the Mystics, averaging 4.0 PPG and 3.6 RPG that season. During her first three years in the league, she was signed and waived multiple times by the Wings and Mystics, and did not have that consistent playing time to be looked at as a reliable rotation player. But, her WNBA journey began to take a favorable turn when she signed with the Phoenix Mercury during the 2022 season. DiLeo spent both the 2022 and 2023 seasons with the Mercury, and in her first year with the team, she experienced her first-ever postseason run. She had 12 points and four rebounds in her WNBA playoff debut against the Las Vegas Aces. In the 2023 season, she averaged 7.9 PPG and 3.9 RPG. She also averaged 15.1 minutes per game (MPG), which was the first time she averaged double-digit minutes for a season. DiLeo also had 14 double-digit scoring games, which was almost three times as many as she had in the previous four seasons (just five such games). After the two seasons with the Mercury, DiLeo signed with the Aces before the start of the 2024 season, and ultimately spent two years with the franchise. In 2024, she averaged 3.7 PPG, 1.9 RPG and 10.7 MPG, and she also had her first career 20-point game. The following season, which was an injury-hampered one that limited her to 20 regular-season games, she averaged 3.0 PPG, 1.8 PPG and 11.3 MPG. But, she played significant minutes during the postseason en route to winning her first WNBA championship. DiLeo’s stints with the Mercury and Aces allowed her to earn more minutes on the court and experience participating in higher-stakes games in the league. She also displayed her value while playing alongside the league’s best bigs like Brittney Griner and A’ja Wilson. After Las Vegas’ 2025 championship season and an offseason clouded by uncertainty due to CBA negotiations, DiLeo took a chance on one of the newest franchises in the league and signed with Portland. As a member of the Fire, DiLeo has had four games of at least 20 points this season, after having only one such game during her career in the league. In addition, she is shooting 38.6 percent from three-point range. DiLeo has always been a crafty and talented scorer around the rim. But, in her time playing professional basketball, whether it is for the WNBA or the Spanish national team in international competition, she added the three-point shot to make it a valuable aspect of her game. In the WNBA, she began shooting three-pointers during her Mercury stint, and has maintained that willingness to let the ball fly. During her four-year college career, she only attempted two three-pointers (per Her Hoop Stats). Now, she has evolved into a quality stretch big who can score from the perimeter and in the interior. Not your average bucket Megan Gustafson dug through her bag and pulled out this move against her former team! LVA-PDX | League Pass | 2026 WNBA Commissioner’s Cup | @coinbase Tap to watch: https://t.co/ytfCPrSijt pic.twitter.com/AxenGc8qLJ — WNBA (@WNBA) June 12, 2026 So smooth, Meg Megan Gustafson gets the three pointer to go and brings her to 2 3PM! PDX-TOR | League Pass Tap to watch: https://t.co/PUx0PNxG0C pic.twitter.com/BzPkI6nBAM — WNBA (@WNBA) May 23, 2026 She is one of the few veterans on a Fire roster that is mostly comprised of younger and less-experienced players. DiLeo, Bridget Carleton and Karlie Samuelson are the only players on the Fire who, entering this season, have at least five years of experience in the league. And then, the team has some newer faces in the WNBA like Carla Leite, Sarah Ashlee Barker and Serah Williams who have shined in Portland so far this season. Po

articles.summary: That girl’s nice. articles._body: That girl’s nice. Olivia Miles pulled the ball back beyond the arc and sized up A’ja Wilson. It didn’t matter that the reigning MVP and defensive player of the year stood between her and the basket. She was going to get this work. The audacity. The swagger. Miles froze Wilson with an in-and-out hesitation, exploded past her right hip, and finished with a finger roll before help could arrive. A few possessions later, she put Jewell Loyd on skates with the same hesi before draining a three. Then, she attacked Wilson again, this time on the block, using a crafty underhand finish to score over the league’s most intimidating defender. Too fast. Too skilled. Too fearless. The Minnesota Lynx dismantled the defending-champion Las Vegas Aces with a rookie who played as if the moment belonged to her. That performance wasn’t just a breakout moment. It was another example of why Miles’ arrival has transformed the rhythm of Minnesota’s offense. With Napheesa Collier returning, the Lynx face an enviable challenge: preserving the pace, pressure and playmaking Miles has introduced while reincorporating one of the league’s most dominant forwards. WNBA! You’re in danger, girl!   Prepped For The Moment Miles’ acceleration is not an accident. It is by design. At TCU, she ran point in a pro-style offense under Mark Campbell that emphasized pick-and-roll actions, live-dribble creation, and floor spacing straight out of a WNBA playbook. In Campbell’s offense, the ball lived in Miles’ hands. She made quick decisions, blending elite vision, creativity with the ball, and fearless attacks on bigs, and the Horned Frogs were better for it. TCU’s offense posted 119.8 points per 100 possessions, eighth in the nation. The same habits that powered that attack- the quick processing, relentless rim pressure, and advanced pick-and-roll reads–have translated seamlessly to Minnesota.   The Impact At 21-6, the Lynx own the league’s best record, and much of that success begins with an offense that looks noticeably different from a year ago. The most striking change isn’t just how much Minnesota scores. It’s how quickly they get there. Last season, the Lynx led the WNBA in scoring, averaging 86.1 points per game, and led the league in offensive rating despite playing at one of the slowest paces in the league (ranked 10th) This season, the Lynx are 2nd in scoring, averaging 91.7 points per game while being first in offensive rating (113.8) and fifth in pace (97.83)–a 3.77 difference, and it’s due to Miles’ and her playstyle. As she pushes the tempo, Minnesota is playing significantly faster while remaining one of the highest scoring teams in the league. The shift is meaningful. The Lynx haven’t sacrificed efficiency for speed. It has increased the number of possessions while remaining one of the league’s most efficient offenses, a reflection of how Miles pressures defenses before they are organized. Under Miles, the Lynx have more spacing. They empty the paint and let Miles attack defenses downhill as shooters are spaced around her for occasional drive-and-kick opportunities. In this five-second clip, no one is in the paint. Miles is as explosive as she is crafty. With her rim pressure, opposing defenses will have to decide whether to contain her or concede open looks from the perimeter. The added spacing has amplified Kayla McBride’s strengths. Few players relocate better than McBride, and Miles consistently rewards those movements by advancing the ball before defenses can recover. Miles’ constant pressure in the paint and rim create opportunities for clean looks for a spot-up shooter like McBride. In the second clip, Courtney Williams is left wide open due to the chaos Miles creates. In the third clip, the Lynx use a high screen-and-roll with Miles and Natasha Howard to exploit a scrambled defense. It’s a simple action, but it illustrates the type of advantage Miles creates before the defense can set. The play ends with Howard finishing, but the real story in the clip is the type of pressure Miles applies before the screen. That pressure is about to become a valuable weapon for Collier.   The Return Few players are better equipped to capitalize on those advantages than Collier. One of the league’s most efficient scorers, ‘Phee can punish switches in the post, attack closeouts, finish as a roller or facilitate from the elbows. With Miles collapsing defenses before Collier even touches the ball, the Lynx may be adding their best player to an offense that’s already evolved. In the opening play of the clip, Collier fires a dime from three to McBride on a backcut with limited spacing. With the additional spacing and cutters such as Howard in lineups, Collier can pick apart defenses when facilitating. With Miles, defenses will have some uncomfortable decisions to make since Miles is a downhill threat who can also create advantages for others with how she surveys the floor. At the 1:51 mark, Collier seals her defender deep in the post before knocking down the fadeaway. Those post touches become even more dangerous alongside Miles. Defenses will have to choose between sending help to Collier or staying home on a guard capable of getting downhill at any moment. Add elite shooters like McBride and Williams around them, and every defensive rotation comes with a cost. There isn’t a clear answer to this conundrum. On a switch, Collier can hunt and attack mismatches. Drop, and Miles drives. Send help, and Minnesota’s shooters feast on clean open looks. Sit on the perimeter, and two elite creators attack the single coverage. This is what makes Collier’s return so intriguing and dangerous. They’re getting ready to add their MVP-caliber forward to an offense that already discovered another way to create advantages. The perfect fit looks like this: One player creates the advantage. The other makes sure the defense pays for it. The Lynx didn’t just survive until Collier returned. They evolved. Now, the rest of the WNBA has to solv

articles.title: Leading by Example: Marina Mabrey is becoming Toronto’s newest star in her biggest role yet
articles.summary: It’s Thursday, June 25, around 9 p.m in Toronto.  Marina Mabrey catches a pass from Julie Allemand, ditches her defender, steps back, and sinks her ninth three-ball of the game. This marks 53 points on the night, tying the all-time WNBA single-game scoring record.  The crowd at Coca-Cola Coliseum
articles._body: It’s Thursday, June 25, around 9 p.m in Toronto. Marina Mabrey catches a pass from Julie Allemand, ditches her defender, steps back, and sinks her ninth three-ball of the game. This marks 53 points on the night, tying the all-time WNBA single-game scoring record. The crowd at Coca-Cola Coliseum is the loudest it’s likely ever been; you could probably hear it in the States. But if you look just past Mabrey, you can see her Toronto Tempo teammates on the bench; they jump up immediately, clapping, cheering, holding up three fingers. Kiki Rice and Teonni Key, two 2026 WNBA draftees, were the first on their feet — likely because they knew the shot was going in. This picture tells a much bigger story, one that both the Tempo front office and Mabrey have to be proud of. Mabrey was Toronto’s sole free agent selection during this year’s expansion draft. General Manager Monica Wright Rogers and the rest of the front office were happy to commit to Mabrey in the form of a two-year, $2.4 million contract. In free agency, they signed Brittney Sykes to a two-year, $2.3 million deal — essentially giving the backcourt duo the keys to lead this team. Neither of them was afraid of the challenge. In a preseason interview with TSN’s Raegan Subban, Mabrey said, “I would say I’m grateful more than anything. When you’re younger, you dream of moments like this… when it happens, it can feel like ‘Oh, this is a lot of responsibility.’ But at the end of the day, I manifested this, I created this in my mind… I think that if I wasn’t capable of it, I wouldn’t have been able to see it. ” After the expansion draft, Wright Rogers also cited Mabrey’s “ fierce, competitive nature ” as one of the reasons Toronto selected her, describing it as something you can’t coach. She’s not only brought that intense spirit and drive to the Tempo, but she’s fallen seamlessly into her biggest role yet as the leader of this new expansion franchise. Now let’s take a look at how she got here.   Mabrey’s Journey to Toronto With the 19th pick in the 2019 WNBA Draft, the Los Angeles Sparks selected Mabrey out of Notre Dame. She was the fifth and final Fighting Irish alum to be selected, joining Jackie Young, Arike Ogunbowale, Brianna Turner, and Jessica Shepard. In college, Mabrey was known for exactly what she’s doing now — shooting at an elite level. She finished her senior year averaging 12.8 points and five assists per game, while shooting above 40 percent from beyond the arc. She didn’t exactly hit the ground running in Los Angeles. She finished her rookie season with only around 12 minutes per game, averaging four points and shooting only 34.4 percent from the field. She was playing behind guards like Chelsea Gray and Riquna Williams with veterans like Nneka Ogwumike and Candace Parker at the helm. Recently, Mabrey recalled her rookie season. Per Ashley Docking of TSN, she stated, “I had a lot of really great vets in LA… I remember Candace challenged me the first couple of days in training camp. I was like ‘Woah…’ But it made me be ready and have more sense of urgency and not second-guess myself.” Her time with the Sparks was short-lived, as they traded her to the Dallas Wings before the 2020 season kicked off. Dallas is where we got to see more of South Bend’s Mabrey, if you will — this could be because she got to reunite with her friend and former Notre Dame teammate, Ogunbowale. Mabrey spent three years with the Wings, and by the third year, had secured herself a more permanent starting spot. She ended her stint averaging 12.5 points, 3.6 rebounds, and three assists per game. After a trade, Mabrey then spent the next season and a half in Chicago. She joined Kahleah Copper and Courtney Williams, becoming a dominant guard trio and the 2023 Sky’s leading scorers. Mabrey averaged 15 points per game in 2023. But by the next season, the team was going through some coaching changes, and she grew unhappy with her role in Chicago. “ I came to play for James Wade, the system he had built and the vision he saw for me,” She told the Chicago Sun-Times. “I don’t like to jump ship, so he left, and then I thought, ‘OK, let’s see what happens’.” Ultimately, as her role shifted, her numbers went down, from scoring to shooting efficiency. Mabrey requested a trade halfway through the 2024 season, with her preferred destination being the Connecticut Sun — making this her fourth team in seven years. She told the Chicago Sun-Times that she felt Connecticut would be a “better situation,” citing it as “ an opportunity for me to get a chance to play with veterans, people who have won a championship.” Those veterans included players like DeWanna Bonner and Alyssa Thomas. When Mabrey joined the Sun, Bonner described her as “a vet and a dynamic scorer… Someone who you know holds her own. We don’t have to stop and teach anything. We could just put her out there, and she’s going to flow really well with us.” Connecticut went on a run in the playoffs before being eliminated by the Minnesota Lynx in Game 5 of the 2024 semifinals. Mabrey finished that season as the Sun’s second-leading scorer, while shooting a career-high 46.7 percent from the floor. Sadly, the Sun’s success came to a halt as 12 of its 15 players from the 2024 season left Connecticut in one way or another. This ultimately pushed Mabrey to request another trade before the start of the 2025 season — it was denied by the Sun. General Manager Jennifer Rizzotti told ESPN that the denial of a trade was “ rooted in a desire to build around her , have her here, have her be the catalyst for what we want to do offensively…” Despite not necessarily wanting to be there, she made the most of her new role, as it likely prepared her for what was coming for her next in Toronto. She and Tina Charles were the pillars of the struggling young 2025 Sun squad. Mabrey conducted the frontcourt with young guards Leïla Lacan, Saniya Rivers, and Jacy Sheldon. articles.summary: We’re just about halfway through the 2026 season, and the standings are looking a bit different than anyone planned for at the beginning of the summer. The bottom half of the W’s teams has managed to stay fairly consistent to what we’ve seen throughout June, but the best in the league continue to
articles._body: We’re just about halfway through the 2026 season, and the standings are looking a bit different than anyone planned for at the beginning of the summer. The bottom half of the W’s teams has managed to stay fairly consistent to what we’ve seen throughout June, but the best in the league continue to shake it up and surpass each other with every passing day. Here’s how it looks as of now. Teams on the Rise Dallas Wings The Dallas Wings are currently on a five-game winning streak, highlighted by road wins against the New York Liberty and Toronto Tempo. Since preseason, the Wings—led by Paige Bueckers, with the help of No. 1 pick Azzi Fudd, Arike Ogunbowale, and new additions Jessica Shepard and Alanna Smith—have been regarded as a dark horse championship contender, and, barring some early season struggles, they’ve proven to be just that. Bueckers and Shepard were named All-Star starters, and the dynamic offensive duo is playing like it: on Tuesday in New York, Shepard dropped her third triple-double of the season, recording 22 points, 12 rebounds, and 11 assists on 11-16 from the field. Three days later, in Montreal, Bueckers scored 34 points, putting on a show for the biggest regular season crowd in WNBA history. With these kinds of performances, plus Fudd continuing to find a groove, the Wings are looking dangerous. Bueckers is playing like the most clutch player in the league, and when she’s hot, there’s no stopping the 2025 No. 1 pick. The team admittedly has a fairly easy schedule waiting for it in the next few weeks, but at the end of the day, wins are wins, and multiple low-ranked teams have demonstrated that they can step up to put on a show. If the Wings can continue with their success and continue to build momentum for when playoff time comes around, we could very well be watching a team with great potential to take down the Liberty or Las Vegas Aces on the biggest stage.   Indiana Fever The Fever have had an interesting 2026 season, to say the least. After the team’s deep playoff run last year, the Winsidr team—and most others—were very high on Indiana, and we ranked them fourth coming into the season. Since then, though, the team has struggled both on and off the court, dropping as low as ninth on our power rankings. Indiana seems to finally be finding its stride, sitting at 14-9, good for 5th in the WNBA. The team has been without All-Star point guard Caitlin Clark for much of the last two weeks, but has still managed to pick up big wins against the Aces and Phoenix Mercury, in addition to beating the Aces again with Clark back on the floor, this time by more than 30 points. 2026 All-Stars Aliyah Boston and Kelsey Mitchell have been balling, the former recording 19 points and 11 rebounds and the latter 27 points against A’ja Wilson and Las Vegas. Indiana is far from where they were projected to be before the season kicked off, but the past few games have been a start. If the team can manage to pick up some revenge wins against the Golden State Valkyries and New York Liberty this week, the league will look entirely different than it did just a few days ago.   Teams on the Decline New York Liberty New York only dropped one spot since last week’s rankings, but the 2024 Champions seem to be struggling greatly. In its last 10 games, New York is a shocking 3-7, racking up losses against should-be unworthy opponents like the Seattle Storm, Washington Mystics, and Los Angeles Sparks while somehow defeating the Minnesota Lynx and the Aces twice, including for the Commissioner’s Cup. There lies the Liberty’s biggest issue: they play up or down to the level of their opponents rather than sticking to the brand of basketball we all know they can and should be playing. Stars Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones—both named 2026 All-Stars—have made multiple pointed statements about the necessity of playing with heart, but it hasn’t stuck yet. The Liberty are now 7th in the WNBA and have to play the Wings and Fever before the All-Star break. Injuries to Satou Sabally and Leonie Fiebich will only make this stretch harder, and New York’s search for consistency and chemistry will have to wait even longer. Roster-wise, this Liberty team is a championship contender, but judging by play alone, they have a lot to work on before even thinking about a playoff run, let alone reaching the Finals.   Atlanta Dream The Atlanta Dream continue to struggle, losing to the Mystics, Valkyries (for the third time in a week), and Portland Fire, and picking up a win against the Seattle Storm since Volume 4. The All-Star trio of Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray, and Angel Reese have each had their ups and downs, and both of the guards have struggled with efficiency in this stretch (Howard scored 10 points on 3-9 shooting and Gray scored 20 points on 8-18 against the Fire). Reese also missed the Dream’s last game with an ankle injury sustained in the team’s win against Seattle two days prior. Much like the Liberty and Fever, the Dream were lauded as serious title contenders ahead of this season, given that the team finished as a three seed in 2025 and went on to add Reese. The Dream have the opportunity to pick up some wins in the next two weeks before the All-Star break, but this brutal losing period is bound to leave a mark on how the team is perceived for the rest of the season: when faced with serious competition like the Golden State Valkyries, the Dream folded and couldn’t even use lower-ranked teams to build morale back up. articles.title: A’ja Wilson soars above the rest of the league this season
articles.summary: A’ja Wilson continues to soar above the WNBA this season, this time thanks to supporting players like NaLyssa Smith.  The tallest structure in Las Vegas is The Strat, standing at 1,114 feet it’s the tallest observation tower in the United States. Anyone who has seen it towering above surrounding
articles._body: A’ja Wilson continues to soar above the WNBA this season, this time thanks to supporting players like NaLyssa Smith. The tallest structure in Las Vegas is The Strat, standing at 1,114 feet it’s the tallest observation tower in the United States. Anyone who has seen it towering above surrounding buildings on the north side of the Strip have seen that its observation deck is propped up by a large support structure. That support provides the base for a restaurant, casino, amusement rides, and is topped by a spire rising even higher above the lights of other resorts. A similar level of support is taking place further south on the Las Vegas Strip inside T-Mobile Arena this season for the city’s defending champions and their biggest star, A’ja Wilson, who is having yet another career year, but this time it is because there’s a supporting cast lifting her up as she soars to new heights. It defies any sort of logic at this point. In 2025, the Aces won their third title in four years, and along the way, Wilson picked up her fourth Most Valuable Player and third Defensive Player of the Year awards. However, the reality is that A’ja is at it again; she was awarded the Western Conference Player of the Month in May, already has two Player of the Week nods, and currently leads the league in points per game and blocks per game. Simply put, she is as dominant now as she has been during her already Hall of Fame worthy career. But if you look beyond the lights, the glam, the shimmer, and the neon (we’re taking this Las Vegas imagery as far as it can go), and dig into what makes A’ja’s tour de force churn in 2026, you find that her success is aided in part by another big on the Vegas roster, NaLyssa Smith. She arrived in Las Vegas via a trade with the Dallas Wings in 2025, coming in exchange for a 2027 first round pick. A former #1 pick herself, NaLyssa entered the league in 2022 as the focal point for several unsuccessful Indiana Fever squads before landing in Dallas, where she struggled to breakthrough in a jumbled rotation of other talented players. She saw her shooting and rebounding stats completely fall off a cliff, and her play seemed to stagnate as well as the Wings struggled through the early part of a season that would not include a trip to the playoffs. But fortunes changed in Vegas as they often do and after the midseason trade, Smith found herself riding high amid a new culture and opportunity to play alongside the most decorated big in the league. She had two double-doubles in her first three games for the Aces, as she saw her statistical output rebound from the career lows she had earlier in the season with Dallas. This season, Smith has elevated her game even more. Her current PPG and RPG averages (11.3 and 6.6, respectively) are her highest since 2023, and she is currently shooting a career high 66.7% from the field. The eyeball test confirms what the numbers say as well. Watching any Aces game, you will see Smith roaming the baseline and paint on offense for a rebound and putback shot or to find space for an easy basket as the defense overcompensates to adjust to the stars elsewhere on the court for Las Vegas. How does this career reassurance for NaLyssa Smith impact how A’ja Wilson operates during another potential MVP season for her? For one, Smith’s high motor and effort play in the paint allow for Wilson to operate more from the midrange and outside the arc. 18 games into this season, she is already approaching her 2025 totals for three point attempts and makes. The paint presence of Smith is also giving A’ja better looks inside the paint. According to Her Hoops Stats, which tracks shooting by different areas of the court, Wilson is currently shooting a career best 81 percent for shots in the restricted area of the paint. We also see in real time how beneficial it is for Smith to have someone as dangerous as A’ja Wilson roaming outside the paint. Whenever a reigning MVP has the ball, the attention of the defense is going there, and Smith can fill the gaps that cause for easy looks for herself, as seen here in a sequence against the Portland Fire. The success doesn’t just come from the attention that Wilson draws, however, as NaLyssa Smith remains a relentless force on the boards. She sits at 15th in the league in offensive rebounding, just behind Wilson, and is one player you will find regularly putting a body on an opponent to box out for a board.   NaLyssa Smith offensive rebound and putback layup #WNBA — Danielle H (@danielleceltics.bsky.social) 2026-06-21T20:42:53.321Z   Ultimately, the success of the Aces comes down to more than these two players, but it is hard to ignore the impact that this duo has had on each other in the past year. In Smith, A’ja has found a reliable post partner who can allow her to work in new areas of the court. In Wilson, NaLyssa has found someone she can play off of in using her energy, instincts, and basketball intelligence to find success and reinvent her career. A’ja Wilson was early to seeing the potential of this partnership, saying in a press conference after NaLyssa Smith’s first double-double as an Ace on July 7, 2025 in what now seems like a prophecy: “When you’re able to share and people are receiving it well, you can continue to pour into them and I hope that we continue to do that for her and let her know how valuable she is to this team.” A player with that much value to the league’s most valuable player has to be worth quite a lot.   The post A’ja Wilson soars above the rest of the league this season appeared first on Winsidr .
