articles.title: What should fans expect if owner Mark Walter also ends up selling the Los Angeles Sparks?
articles.summary: Mark Walter, the controlling owner of the Los Angeles Sparks, is in a heap of financial trouble. The Wall Street Journal reported that the federal government is investigating him for fraud involving $16 billion in private credit deals with his insurance companies. While that investigation is ongoing
articles._body: Sparks fans and Nneka Ogwumike. | NBAE via Getty Images Mark Walter, the controlling owner of the Los Angeles Sparks, is in a heap of financial trouble. The Wall Street Journal reported that the federal government is investigating him for fraud involving $16 billion in private credit deals with his insurance companies. While that investigation is ongoing, it’s clear he’s feeling the heat. Walter sold the Los Angeles Lakers to Bob Iger and Josh Kusher after owning them for under a year. The Athletic reported this week that he is also looking to sell his minority ownership share of Chelsea. Given that Walter also owns the Sparks, could they be next on the chopping block? So far, no. The Sparks weren’t at all connected to the sale of the Lakers, and there have been no indications that he’s shopping them. Source tells me the Los Angeles Sparks are not a part of any sale — Dan Woike (@DanWoikeSports) August 12, 2026 However, this is a developing story. Until the dust has settled on Walter’s fire sale and the federal investigation, one can’t assume it will be business as usual in Los Angeles. And with the WNBA growing at an unprecedented level, no new expansion bids on the horizon and Walter feeling financial pressure, that’s a scenario that could entice someone to make a call and try to purchase the Sparks. So, what happens if Walter does sell them? Well, it’d be messy, but this is a great time for a change in ownership. The Sparks have already secured another losing season, making it six in a row. On Thursday, they lost their sixth game in a row, allowing the Atlanta Dream to score a franchise-record 124 points in the rout at crypto.com Arena. Final. pic.twitter.com/dKAUauNgof — Los Angeles Sparks (@LASparks) August 21, 2026 They’ve all but officially been eliminated from the playoffs, making this the longest postseason drought in franchise history. Things haven’t been working for a while, and this team that was built to win now instead continuing their recent stretch of losing seasons proved to be the final straw. LA began cleaning house due to these failures. They parted ways with general manager Reagan Pebley back in July, and traded superstar Kelsey Plum right before the trade deadline. Farhan Zaidi, a special advisor to Walter, spoke to Bill Plaschke of the Los Angeles Times about a need to change direction for the Sparks, admitting: We pushed in a lot of chips this year, and we had good reason to do that, but the reality is it hasn’t gone as we’d hoped or expected. Now we have to be open for anything. Everything has to be on the table for us. We have to take a long-term perspective rather than focusing on the rest of the season. Exclusive: Inside the Los Angeles Sparks’ Thursday morning shootaround practice before hosting the Atlanta Dream. LA Sparks head coach Lynne Roberts told me her team will be relatively healthy but ownership has asked that bench players receive playing time for rest of season.… pic.twitter.com/rjSjXSxN7C — John W. Davis (@johnwdavis) August 20, 2026 More changes are guaranteed for next year as well. Nneka Ogwumike announced her retirement earlier this week, leaving this franchise with no All-Stars heading into 2027 while also removing another veteran. They have two first-round picks in the upcoming draft, so the intention is to get younger and hit the reset button on the rebuild….once again. If there were ever a time where a new ownership could come in and not negatively disrupt things for the Sparks, that’d be now. Still, that doesn’t mean a change would be easy. The Sparks to-do list this offseason is long. Walter or a new owner must hire a general manager, and that person will have to decide whether head coach Lynne Roberts should remain in her role. Typically, a new general manager means a new head coach. Roberts has been the coach in LA for two seasons and has gone 33-46 over that span. Beyond front office decisions, coaching personnel and draft selections, the Sparks also need to finish the practice facility currently under development . Would a new owner commit to that project, or would they have different plans that could delay things? The LA Sparks have unveiled plans to build a $150M practice facility in El Segundo. It's the largest investment for a single team in the history of women’s sports. pic.twitter.com/Wi0fgjjtfw — Front Office Sports (@FOS) September 24, 2025 Whoever owns the Sparks in 2027 has their work cut out for them. This is an iconic franchise. One of the originals, dating back to when the WNBA was born. It deserves an owner who puts their focus and care into it and wants to bring it back into relevance. Maybe that’s Walter. Or perhaps he sells, and someone else embraces the challenges. Either way, Sparks fans don’t care who the owner is. They care if they’ll get the job done and bring back winning basketball to Los Angeles. When the Sparks last won a home playoff game in 2019, their arena was still called STAPLES Center. That’s an embarrassing fact—and one that needs to change expeditiously.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Even with a 12-game losing streak, the Toronto Tempo, not the Portland Fire, are the 2026 expansion winners
articles.summary: The Toronto Tempo skid into Vancouver on a 12-game losing streak, now 15 games under .500 and officially eliminated from playoff contention. Their expansion opponent on Friday night (10 p.m. ET, ION), the Portland Fire, are holding steady in the No. 9 spot in the WNBA standings, a respectable five g
articles._body: Brittney Sykes. | NBAE via Getty Images The Toronto Tempo skid into Vancouver on a 12-game losing streak, now 15 games under .500 and officially eliminated from playoff contention. Their expansion opponent on Friday night (10 p.m. ET, ION), the Portland Fire, are holding steady in the No. 9 spot in the WNBA standings, a respectable five games under .500. Heyyyy Vancouver 🌊 Did you miss us? Because we missed you! pic.twitter.com/AlEopQuRea — Toronto Tempo (@TempoBasketball) August 20, 2026 Of the 2026 expansion teams, Portland, clearly, is the greater success, right? That Toronto is falling far short of the postseason ambitions they loudly announced, whereas Portland expressed no such bold intentions, only underscores that the Fire are the expansion “winners.” I might have to disagree with that seemingly obvious assessment. Entering the season, I was skeptical of the Tempo’s approach. I thought they overspent on their million-dollar backcourt of Marina Mabrey and Brittney Sykes, too eagerly investing in the imagined superstar potential of two players who had been inconsistent offensive options during their WNBA careers. Marina, Slim and the Tempo proved me wrong. Mabrey has proven to be the perfect star for Canada’s first WNBA team, something Zack Ward presciently foresaw . She was a surefire All-Star, having authored the most memorable single-game performance of the 2026 season when she ignited for a record-tying 53 points. Sykes was on track to join Mabrey in Chicago if not for a foot injury that robbed her of a second-straight All-Star nod. Sykes’ injury, from which she just returned two games ago after missing 18 games, was the pivot point for Toronto. One game under .500 with Slim, Toronto has tanked since then, increasingly unable to overcome accumulating injuries. Slim really said 'GUESS WHO'S BACK'😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/5vvzr707uQ — Toronto Tempo (@TempoBasketball) August 18, 2026 However, the Mabrey-Sykes backcourt, in addition to the ready-to-go rookie Kiki Rice, have provided enough of a proof of concept for Toronto. No, it’s no the best backcourt in the league, but it’s good enough, with better health and an improved supporting cast, to become the foundation for a genuine playoff contender. Had Sykes stayed healthy, it’s easy to imagine the Tempo hanging around the edges of the playoff race, encouraging them to make a more aggressive frontcourt upgrade at the trade deadline. Now, that roster refurbishment can happen in the offseason. And if the lottery gods bless the Tempo with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 WNBA Draft, Toronto could be quite dangerous. With the Tempo loss tonight + Sky win, they've swapped places in the reverse standings. Toronto now holds the second-best odds (24%) of securing the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft lottery. Chicago drops to third (16%). Connecticut Sun also won tonight. pic.twitter.com/UrJCcxXq9l — Zulfi Sheikh (@zulfi_sheikh) August 19, 2026 Even if that optimistic outcome doesn’t materialize, I still have to admit to being too skeptical of Toronto’s plan. Going for it out of the gate with a pair of star-caliber guards has the Tempo prepared to be competitive in today’s WNBA, where things often change fast . So, while I’m inclined to support the processes implemented in Portland, where, instead of chasing an immediate postseason high, they were intent upon building a program that, eventually, would produce a consistent winner, I do wonder if slow and steady actually wins the race. In modern sports, it’s seen as “smart” to value process over results, but teams, from executives to coaches to players, are judged on results. 🔥 practice pic.twitter.com/sBpKfGTH2l — Portland Fire (@theportlandfire) August 19, 2026 The Fire likely will continue to garner praise ( including from these parts ) for their emphasis on player development, head coach Alex Sarama’s innovative coaching strategies and a commitment to culture. Yet, all that good process might just result in them remaining a plucky, hard-playing team that never advances into a playoff threat that has to be taken seriously. Adding a star-level player or two, the prerequisite for true postseason success, could change the calculation for Portland, although it would also be a deviation from the organization’s prevailing approach. Presuming the Fire do not make a late-breaking playoff push this season, I would predict that the Tempo, not the Fire, become the first team of the expansion class of 2026 to make the playoffs. That, in turn, makes them expansion “winners,” even if the Tempo, without Mabrey (adductor), Nyara Sabally (calf) and María Conde (calf), lose for a 13th-straight time on Friday night. (Introducing a pair of mascots also gives them some bonus credit.) Canada, they’re home! A warm welcome for Dez & Dot. Official Mascot Reveal presented by @TurboTaxCanada pic.twitter.com/lwf6JGjACX — Toronto Tempo (@TempoBasketball) August 19, 2026 I can confirm per sources that Dez and Dot, the Tempo mascots, are neither siblings OR dating. Just besties 😂 — chelsea leite (@chelsealeite) August 19, 2026 How would you assess the two expansion teams? Do you see the ideal vision, confirmed by a playoff berth, coming together first in Toronto or Portland? In today’s WNBA, should all teams just go for it, with winning now prioritized over everything? Can a more measured team build actually come to fruition when things seem to change so fast and frequently?

Those dynamics included a fight for respect, both with
articles._body: Head coach Geno Auriemma speaks to President Bill Clinton after winning the 1995 national championship. | Getty Images On Friday, Aug. 21, “The Dynasty: UConn Huskies” debuts on Apple TV. Our Zack Ward already has reviewed the three-part docuseries, positively assessing how it captures all the dynamics behind UConn’s rise to women’s college basketball dominance. Those dynamics included a fight for respect, both within UConn athletics and into larger sports culture. Swish Appeal is thrilled to share an exclusive clip from the docuseries that introduces how head coach Geno Auriemma navigated and challenged the sports world’s sexist attitudes towards women’s sports as his program was emerging as a women’s college basketball powerhouse. The exclusive clip also includes commentary from Jeff Goldberg, a former Hartford Courant beat writer who covered the team in the early 2000s. Zack just interviewed Goldberg about his experience on the Huskies beat, offering even more insight into how UConn became “The Dynasty.”

articles.title: Interview: Former Hartford Courant beat writer Jeff Goldberg offers intriguing insight into ‘The Dynasty: UConn Huskies’ docuseries
articles.summary: Former Hartford Courant UConn women’s basketball beat writer Jeff Goldberg, author of Bird at the Buzzer and Unrivaled, serves as a key voice in the docuseries, “The Dynasty: UConn Huskies,” which comes out on Apple TV on Friday, Aug. 21. He was kind enough to sit down with Swish Appeal before the g
articles._body: Head coach Geno Auriemma, Diana Taurasi and the UConn Huskies wait to be introduced before the 2004 national championship game. | Getty Images Former Hartford Courant UConn women’s basketball beat writer Jeff Goldberg, author of Bird at the Buzzer and Unrivaled , serves as a key voice in the docuseries, “The Dynasty: UConn Huskies,” which comes out on Apple TV on Friday, Aug. 21. He was kind enough to sit down with Swish Appeal before the global release to give his take on the series and why it is so important. The series tells the story of UConn from the time that Geno Auriemma first took the head coaching job in Storrs in 1985. Over the four NCAA-era years before he took over, UConn went 35-74. They shared a fieldhouse with the track and field team. Goldberg says they had to put netting up to prevent the shot putters from hitting the court, and that athletes were running around the track during basketball games. Even Goldberg, who was born and raised in Connecticut, needed a refresher on these details from the early days, as the Huskies women’s basketball program has, of course, come a long way. That’s why “The Dynasty” was made: to tell the full story. Goldberg covered perhaps the most crucial years of Auriemma’s program: 2001-02 to 2005-06. He witnessed the national championship total rise from two to five. At the time he left the beat, the Huskies were neck-and-neck with the Tennessee Lady Volunteers, who had six. Swish Appeal asked Goldberg what viewers will learn from the docuseries, his perspective on the Auriemma-Pat Summitt relationship, where Diana Taurasi ranks on his all-time UConn list, what it was like watching Sue Bird and Taurasi together in 2002, what UConn’s attitude was when they didn’t win it all and why it is so important to tell the story of women’s basketball from the beginning. Here are some highlights from our conversation: On where Diana Taurasi ranks among the all-time greatest Huskies: Alright, look … I’m obviously horrendously biased, because I got to see almost all of her games. Up close. I grew up in Connecticut, and I was a teenager throughout the 1980s. So my hero of all sports heroes was Larry Bird. And you know (there was) the famous thing at his retirement ceremony, where Magic (Johnson)’s like, “There’ll never ever be another Larry Bird.” Well, that’s not true—there was another Larry Bird. She didn’t wear 33; she just wore 3. I mean (Diana) shot like Larry Bird, she had the range of Larry Bird, she had incredible passing like Larry Bird, she trash-talked like Larry Bird, and she was as clutch as any player I have ever seen. She embodied everything about him. And I used to goof on her, because, you know, she’s from Chino, CA, so who was her favorite player? It was Magic. And I’m like, “No no no, Larry. Your favorite player should be Larry” So for me—and this is nothing against Maya Moore, this is nothing against Breanna Stewart, it’s nothing against Paige Bueckers, it’s nothing against Rebecca Lobo, or her teammate Sue Bird—Diana Taurasi is the greatest basketball player I ever saw. Men or women. She was just the best. And a personality to match. One of my favorite people.   Diana left an undeniable mark on the game. Now, the next generation is putting that legacy into words. #NCAAWBB x 🎥 @phoenixmercury pic.twitter.com/ifC1myVHpO — NCAA March Madness (@MarchMadnessWBB) August 17, 2026 On why it’s important to learn the full history of women’s basketball: It’s what drove me to write the two books that I wrote. Women’s basketball—for every good reason you can think of—their focus is as forward-thinking as possible….Even now….Collegiate women’s basketball is as popular as it’s ever been, but they’re still fighting for that seat at the table…. So I don’t think they feel like they have time to kind of take a breath and take a step back and look at the history that they are creating all the time. There’s so much incredible history in the women’s game. And forget UConn—I mean you can go all the way back. Go back to Cheryl Miller, go back to that Texas team in ’86, the first team that went undefeated. There are stories and teams that women’s basketball fans have no idea about that are as compelling as anything that they did at UConn…. There’s a tremendous history that is just waiting to be told. And hopefully this (documentary) is the start of that.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: Despite the Dallas Wings’ recent slide and Azzi Fudd’s season-ending injury, fans should still be encouraged—and here’s why
articles.summary: With eight games remaining in the Dallas Wings’ 2026 regular-season schedule, it’s worth referring back to Zack Ward’s season preview of the team. The theme of Zack’s preseason analysis of Dallas? Patience. He examined the history of teams with back-to-back No. 1 picks in WNBA drafts, noting that am
articles._body: Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers. | Getty Images With eight games remaining in the Dallas Wings’ 2026 regular-season schedule, it’s worth referring back to Zack Ward’s season preview of the team. The theme of Zack’s preseason analysis of Dallas? Patience. He examined the history of teams with back-to-back No. 1 picks in WNBA drafts, noting that among the 2024 Indiana Fever, 2018 Las Vegas Aces, 2016 Seattle Storm and 2002 Storm, only one team—the 2002 Storm with Sue Bird and Lauren Jackson—finished with a winning record. Of the more recent teams, the 2024 Fever’s .500 record is the best mark. Zack thus pondered : So should expectations  really  be that high for the 2026 Dallas Wings, as they, like those teams did, pursue success with their back-to-back No. 1 picks? Probably not. But even with just one No. 1 pick overall on the roster, the spotlight is always going to be on your organization. So, the big question for the Wings in 2026 should be simple: Can Dallas demonstrate significant improvement? I think Zack was right on. Steady improvement, not a stratospheric leap in the standings, was a reasonable goal for the 2026 Wings. Zack forecasted a 16-28 record as most likely, while allowing for some paths that could put the Wings on the cusp of a playoff berth. Well, the Wings have soared past those expectations. REALLY LIKE THAT 🧨 pic.twitter.com/bYry0UgsLM — Dallas Wings (@DallasWings) August 15, 2026 And, that’s the problem. Currently four games over .500 at 20-16, Dallas is on track for the best-ever season by a franchise that picked first overall in two consecutive drafts. But, the sentiment around the team is suggestive of anything but success. Disappointment and disillusionment define Dallas. The trajectory of the Wings’ season explains the current malaise. Yet, it shouldn’t excuse it. After a couple of ugly defensive outings that led to some early losses, Dallas found their groove, establishing an effective offensive attack that propelled the team to as high as fourth in the WNBA standings. A pre-All-Star break surge, as the team cruised into the Chicago festivities on a 7-1 stretch, seemed to presage an even more ascendant finish to the season. WINGSSSSSS WIN 🤪🤪 pic.twitter.com/erujuLqZX8 — Dallas Wings (@DallasWings) July 23, 2026 Dallas, of course, has stumbled, with their 2-7 post-All-Star record inspiring all the agita about the team. Still, in the bigger picture, the Wings, long one of the WNBA’s more incompetent organizations, are right where they’re supposed to be based on the back-to-back No. 1 pick histories cited by Zack. A team only has two-straight top picks if they’ve been bad. Escaping that ineptitude, even with top talents, not only takes time, but also is not linear. There are going to by ups and downs as an organization experiments with the best way to maximize their precious prospects. For Dallas, Jessica Shepard has proven an effective offensive partner for Paige Bueckers, earning an All-Star starter honor as she piled up impressive offensive stats as a fully-empowered fulcrum for the Wings. Shepard, however, has significant defensive deficiencies, ones the Dallas leadership attempted to mitigate with Alanna Smith, last year’s co-Defensive Player of the Year. Smith, however, has experienced a mostly-cursed season in Dallas, with her integration and effectiveness limited by injuries. It’s also been another uneven season for Arike Ogunbowale, with her fluctuating offensive usage and effectiveness injecting unpredictability, rather than veteran stability, into the team. Two All-Star peas in a pod 🫛 pic.twitter.com/Kl7rOEH4DO — Dallas Wings (@DallasWings) July 26, 2026 The performance of those key veterans, plus other members of the Dallas supporting cast, is data that can be evaluated and then applied over the offseason so the Wings remain on, or ahead of, the top-pick trajectories mapped out by the 2002 Storm, 2016 Storm, 2018 Aces and 2024 Fever. The Bird-Jackson Storm won two titles (2004, 2010), the Jewell Loyd-Breanna Stewart Storm also captured two championships (2018, 2020), the A’ja Wilson-Jackie Young Aces have three titles (2022, 2023, 2025) and many project the Aliyah Boston-Caitlin Clark Fever to eventually raise a banner. And to re-emphasize, the Wings, despite their recent woes and their inconsistent supporting players, are on pace to finish with a better first season record than any of those teams. It is, however, slightly alarming that Azzi Fudd is undergoing a season-ending knee procedure after missing the Wings’ last five games with knee soreness, especially since the issue is with her right knee, the knee on which she suffered ACL and meniscus tears in 2023. Nevertheless, it was encouraging to see the impact the first pick in the 2026 draft made for her team. The Wings went 19-11 in games in which Azzi played. So, that’s one win without her. Ideally, the team would be able to survive without their star rookie. But, she is a star rookie. Her absence is not inconsequential. Dallas Wings rookie guard Azzi Fudd will undergo an arthroscopic procedure to address ongoing right knee soreness, the team announced today. Fudd will have the procedure done in Connecticut early next week and will begin rehabbing immediately. With less than five weeks remaining… — Dallas Wings PR (@DallasWingsPR) August 19, 2026 Overall, the Wings had been at their best with Fudd on the court, with a +4.7 scoring margin per game in Azzi’s minutes. Bueckers ranks second in plus-minus on the team, with Dallas winning by an average of +2.6 points per game in her minutes. As Dallas aims to make sure Paige and Azzi become yet another No. 1 pick pairing to win multiple titles, their on-court effective is what matters most. Health, at present, is the only potentially concerning crack in Dallas’ Bueckers-Fudd foundation. Of course, in the immediate, it would still be nice to see the Wings rediscover some of their early-season rhythm ahead of the playoffs,

articles.title: Defined by grace and greatness, Nneka Ogwumike announces she will retire from the WNBA at the end of the season
articles.summary: On June 2, before the Los Angeles Sparks took on the Las Vegas Aces, I conducted an exclusive interview with Nneka Ogwumike and asked her how many more seasons she thought she had left. Her response was short. “I don’t know,” Ogwumike said. Well, two months later, she knows. On Tuesday morning, in a
articles._body: Nneka Ogwumike. | Getty Images On June 2, before the Los Angeles Sparks took on the Las Vegas Aces, I conducted an exclusive interview with Nneka Ogwumike and asked her how many more seasons she thought she had left. Her response was short. “I don’t know,” Ogwumike said. Well, two months later, she knows. On Tuesday morning, in an interview with Boardroom’s Taylor Rooks, Ogwumike shocked the basketball world by announcing that her WNBA career would be over at the end of this season. EXCLUSIVE: @nnekaogwumike is calling it a career after this season. pic.twitter.com/wrvFCQpGcK — Boardroom (@boardroom) August 19, 2026 Via a Sparks press release , Ogwumike elaborated on her looming retirement: I’ve learned there’s power in knowing when to walk away. For so long, that strength meant finding a way to keep pushing. Now, it means recognizing when you feel complete. I find myself grateful, fulfilled, and at peace with everything this game has given me and everything I’ve poured into it. As Ogwumike is one of the league’s most legendary players, as well as the WNBPA president, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert congratulated Ogwumike on retirement, releasing a statement that read: There is no telling the story of the WNBA’s recent growth and evolution without Nneka Ogwumike. Her extraordinary career has been defined not only by excellence, but by the way she has led and lifted those around her. She is a champion and MVP, one of the most accomplished players of all time, and a fierce competitor who has represented the very best our game has to offer. For 15 seasons, Nneka has led with grace and conviction, competed with an unmistakable spark, and carried herself with a generosity and thoughtfulness that have earned the admiration of everyone across our game. Nneka will retire at the end of this season leaving the WNBA much better than she found it—a testament not only to the player she has been, but to the person and leader she is. I have been fortunate to work closely with Nneka over the years and have been inspired by her passion and unwavering commitment to the players. It has been a privilege to watch her remarkable journey, and while there is still more basketball to be played this season, we congratulate her on an extraordinary career and look forward to celebrating her in the months ahead. WNBA Statement on Nneka Ogwumike's Retirement pic.twitter.com/8TfBzGWcBg — WNBA Communications (@WNBAComms) August 19, 2026 Ogwumike accomplished everything possible in the WNBA. She was the No. 1 overall pick in 2012 WNBA Draft by the Sparks. Ogwumike was selected to an All-WNBA team on eight occasions, in addition to achieving 11 All-Star honors—including in 2026. That’s tied for the second-most All-Star appearances ever in the WNBA. She was MVP in 2016, the same season where she helped led the Sparks to the organization’s last championship. This year, in her return to the Sparks after two seasons with the Seattle Storm, Ogwumike is averaging 16.9 points, 8.7 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.1 steals per game. Her most notable moment was her game-winner against the Liberty. She also became the franchise’s all-time leading scorer. There weren't many highs this year for Nneka Ogwumike and the Sparks, but her game-winner over the Liberty was fantastic. https://t.co/5tUjyN4U93 — Edwin Garcia (@ECreates88) August 19, 2026 Following the announcement of her retirement, Ogwumike received an infinite amount of social media flowers, headlined by love from her sister Chiney. 15 seasons! ✨ With you every step of the way… and it still feels like we’re just getting started! ❤️ Congrats to the best big sister in the world, @nnekaogwumike ! 💐 pic.twitter.com/kRtbu2pCuU — Chiney Ogwumike (@chiney) August 19, 2026 Angel Reese’s post following Nneka Ogwumike's WNBA retirement announcement: “…Your 15 years in this league were FLAWLESS but somehow the person you are off the court speaks even louder than everything you accomplished on.” ❤️❤️ pic.twitter.com/SeMxUI338y — Angel Report🌹 (@AngelReportt) August 19, 2026 1- Thank you Nneka. You are the epitome of class, grace and like your name-a tireless warrior. I am grateful to you for so much, for so long. 2-Houston, your hometown gets team next season. Please join ownership group. We still need you. @nnekaogwumike pic.twitter.com/KATRUn0tDV — Holly Rowe (@sportsiren) August 19, 2026 All of us to Nneka right now: But let me know, what are yall saying to Prez/what do yall want to say? pic.twitter.com/ax7yrR4LFb — Arielle (Ari) Chambers (@ariivory) August 19, 2026 Nneka Ogwumike will be eligible as a player for the Class of 2029. Her impact has been felt on and off the court. 🏀 #29HoopClass pic.twitter.com/bvaFJ3Fevk — Basketball HOF (@Hoophall) August 19, 2026 While Ogwumike’s WNBA career is coming to an end, her playing time isn’t. According to Colin Salao of Front Office Sports , Ogwumike will still play in Project B in 2027 . Ogwumike will also remain WNBPA president until executive committee elections are held at the end of the calendar year, as The IX Sports’ Jackie Powell reported. Now that her retirement is official, her end is clear. Ogwumike will play nine more games with the Sparks, and her final one will be on Sept. 24 in Los Angeles against the Golden State Valkyries.

articles.title: WNBA gameday discussion: By finally beating the Minnesota Lynx, the Golden State Valkyries can burnish their championship credentials
articles.summary: When the Golden State Valkyries host WNBA All-Star 2027, the organization certainly would be satisfied if a championship banner was hanging over the Chase Center court. To make it conceivable that such a Bay Area dream could become a reality, they must win on Wednesday night, when they welcome the a
articles._body: Veronica Burton and Kiah Stokes defend Olivia Miles. | NBAE via Getty Images When the Golden State Valkyries host WNBA All-Star 2027, the organization certainly would be satisfied if a championship banner was hanging over the Chase Center court. To make it conceivable that such a Bay Area dream could become a reality, they must win on Wednesday night, when they welcome the arguable title favorites, the league-leading Minnesota Lynx, into Ballhalla (10 p.m. ET, USA Network). WNBay Area 🌟 @WNBA All-Star 2027 is coming to Ballhalla. pic.twitter.com/qdh4p024rS — Golden State Valkyries (@valkyries) August 18, 2026 For a team that has obliterated all expectations since arriving in the league last season, including already clinching a 2026 playoff berth with their Monday night victory over the Dallas Wings, beating Minnesota has proven to be an impossible task. Literally. The Valkyries are 0-8 against the Lynx, losing to Minnesota six times last season—four times in the regular season before falling in a 2-0 sweep in the first round of the playoffs—and twice this season. Golden State can at least take some solace in the fact that they’ve been competitive in almost every contest. While they were pounded by the Lynx in Game 1 of the playoffs, the first-ever playoff game in franchise history, they otherwise suffered a loss no worse than 11 points last season. This season, they’ve lost by three and six points, respectively. Coming close, however, is not going to result in a banner being raised in Chase Center. Built in Year One. Back in Year Two. After becoming the first expansion team in @WNBA history to clinch a playoff berth last season, the Valkyries are headed back to the postseason in Year 2. @aboutKP | 2026 Playoffs pic.twitter.com/dAh9MSAgNb — Golden State Valkyries (@valkyries) August 18, 2026 And as a Eric Nemchock recently highlighted , the Valkyries’ trouble with the Lynx is an indicator of Golden State’s inability to reach the higher level required to beat the W’s very best teams, as five of their nine losses have come against the Lynx and Las Vegas Aces. It’s a blemish on the regular-season resume that doesn’t bode well for the postseason upside, albeit one that can be diminished if they can manage to defeat the Lynx. The team is unlikely to indicate any anxiousness about specifically rectifying their record against Minnesota, as head coach Natalie Nakase had no time to feign enthusiasm about the the team clinching a playoff berth. Instead, expect the Valkyries to insist that this is just another regular-season game that stands as an opportunity to improve, even if Golden State already has hinted at an eagerness to claim that elusive win over Minnesota. Nakase on if she’s able to enjoy this moment given the historic precedent they are setting: “It’s just not my thing. And I don’t want to be fake. And goal is to be the team that wins their last game in the season. That's the goal, and so with that, this is part of the process…” https://t.co/y04z4FYMgI — Kenzo Fukuda (@kenzofuku) August 18, 2026 As is the wont of Nakase, she implemented intentional defensive strategies in both games against the Lynx. The first time around, the Valkyries essentially dared Olivia Miles to beat them, particularly permitting her to fire away from beyond the arc. To that point, the precocious rookie was struggling with her 3-ball. But invited to shoot from deep by Golden State’s defensive scheme, Liv took full advantage and busted out of her early-season slump with a rookie-record eight triples. Her then season-high 28 points, plus seven assists to just one turnover, led the Lynx to the win. Valkyries have gapped Olivia Miles in the 1H, and she’s made them pay each time. Miles is 5/5 from 3P through 1.5 quarters…👀 @ThePodiumFinish — Conrado Pascual (@CP3_777) June 5, 2026 Olivia Miles was made for the big leagues 💪 She set a new rookie record with 8 threes in a game passing Caitlin Clark and Crystal Robinson. Miles also tied the Lynx franchise record for three-pointers in a regular season game. She finished the night with 28 PTS (career-high),… pic.twitter.com/3zXWIunQ6V — WNBA (@WNBA) June 5, 2026 In the rematch, Golden State, fully aware that Miles was not some early-season rookie wonder, gave her their full attention, holding her to a season-low seven points on 1-for-10 shooting from the field, including 0-for-4 from 3. The Valkyries’ D also caused her to cough up six turnovers to four assists. Yet, the rest of the Lynx stepped up as the rook struggled, with Nia Coffey scoring a season-best 22 points as Courtney Williams registered the 21-point and 12-rebound double-double to notch another Minnesota win. #Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase on the adjustments the team needs to make against Olivia Miles/Lynx: “We got to guard her. We didn’t guard her last time.” pic.twitter.com/5Z39jWXmsQ — Nathan Canilao (@nathancanilao) June 20, 2026 Cheryl Reeve on Olivia Miles game against the the Valkyries and what GS did to make her struggle at times “Us and them are the two best defensive teams in the league, so what she saw is actual defense. She saw physicality… she needed a game like this, this was a tremendous… pic.twitter.com/cgylp3up8n — Andrew Dukowitz (@adukeMN) June 20, 2026 Now, Golden State must contend with Napheesa Collier, in addition to all Minnesota’s other weapons. And Phee loves playing the Valkyries. In six career games against Golden State, both in the regular season and postseason, Collier has averaged 21.5 points, her highest scoring average against any opponent. She’s hit 48 percent of her 3s against Golden State, and almost 58 percent all her field goal attempts. So, Nakase and the Valkyrie defense may have devised a solve for Miles, but they’ve yet to figure out Phee. articles.title: How these three young WNBA players are elevating the championship-hopeful Fever, Valkyries and Liberty
articles.summary: When it comes to the WNBA’s playoff-caliber teams, it’s natural to gravitate towards the big names. Teams like the Indiana Fever, Golden State Valkyries and New York Liberty are not short on star players, and it’s easy to give them most of the attention as they keep winning games. Even on these vete
articles._body: Makayla Timpson has turned out to be the perfect fit next to the Indiana Fever’s star players. | NBAE via Getty Images When it comes to the WNBA’s playoff-caliber teams, it’s natural to gravitate towards the big names. Teams like the Indiana Fever, Golden State Valkyries and New York Liberty are not short on star players, and it’s easy to give them most of the attention as they keep winning games. Even on these veteran-laden squads, though, there are a handful of younger players who have made valuable contributions. Let’s give these first- and second-year players their flowers as their teams continue to jockey for playoff position. Makayla Timpson (Indiana Fever) For some young players, it’s not a question of if they’ll get an opportunity, but when. For Timpson, that moment came in a mid-July Fever win over Seattle, in which she eclipsed 30 minutes on the court for the first time in her career. Since then, she’s averaging 7.5 points, 6.0 rebounds and 1.8 defensive stats in 26.3 minutes per game. She’s also drawn starts in each of her last four games, and if she keeps up her current level of play, that doesn’t seem like a role she’ll surrender any time soon. Timpson’s numbers may not be eye-popping, but taken within the context of the Fever’s roster, it’s easier to understand how she’s gotten to this point. The offseason acquisitions of veterans Monique Billings and Myisha Hines-Allen ensured that the Fever would not be lacking for frontcourt partners for perennial All-Star Aliyah Boston, and they also suggested that Timpson would have to raise her game if she was going to become a mainstay in the team’s rotation. Fortunately, Timpson’s skillset and athleticism make her an ideal pairing with Boston, as well as with the Fever’s high-octane backcourt of Kelsey Mitchell and Caitlin Clark. That trio of players is going to handle most of Indiana’s offensive burden, and all their teammates need to do is find ways to play off of them. For Timpson, that means running the floor and simply making herself available around the paint; she did plenty of this in the Fever’s most recent win over Atlanta, a game in which Timpson scored a career-high 20 points. One gets the feeling that this is only the beginning for the energetic forward. Kaitlyn Chen (Golden State Valkyries) We’ve written plenty about the Valkyries’ success this season, namely how their fearsome defense and opportunistic offense has them near the top of the WNBA standings. And while Golden State isn’t lacking for big names, the Valkyries are perhaps a little more reliant on their depth than some of the league’s other top teams, so their bench players deserve some shine for the run the team has been on. Chen has an unenviable task—backing up the league’s reigning Most Improved Player, Veronica Burton—but she handles it well. Picked near the end of the 2025 WNBA Draft, Chen has solidified her role as Golden State’s backup point guard, and she’s made significant strides since her rookie season. While much of the Valkyries’ offensive approach is to simply make fewer mistakes than the other team, Chen has looked much more confident in her second year, more than doubling the number of shots she attempts per game (5.2, up from 2.1 in 2025). It helps that those shots are going in, too. Chen is shooting a highly efficient 54.7 percent from the field, up from just 38 percent in her rookie season. “She has no fear,” Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase said of Chen , pointing to the guard’s ability to attack the basket and finish with either hand. Chen is shooting a remarkable 75.5 percent in the restricted area this season and 45.8 percent on non-restricted area paint attempts—both excellent numbers, especially for a guard. Is Chen going to win a playoff series by herself? That seems unlikely. Her scoring efficiency and care with the basketball (1.2 turnovers in 14.6 minutes per game) are key cogs in Golden State’s offense, however, and the fact that Nakase has been able to turn to Chen for extended periods will pay dividends when it’s time for Burton to play heavier minutes. Pauline Astier (New York Liberty) When the Liberty signed Astier to her first-ever WNBA contract this past offseason, the idea was to have her come off the bench and spell starting guards Sabrina Ionescu and Leonie Fiebich. They probably didn’t envision having such major injury issues: Ionescu has played in 22 of New York’s 36 games, while Fiebich has played in just 14. That may not be what Astier signed up for, but she’s taken full advantage of the opportunity nonetheless. An undrafted rookie from France, Astier has been a steadying hand of sorts for the injury-plagued Liberty. She’s played in all 36 games and started 31 of them, and began her career playing 26.2 minutes per game in May—a crucial number for a team that was without one of the biggest stars, Ionescu, for nearly the entire month. Astier’s minutes have dipped a bit since then as the Liberty have gotten (somewhat) healthier, but she’s remained a solidly productive player. On the season, she’s averaging 9.4 points and 3.5 assists per game while shooting 55.4 percent from the field with Liberty head coach Chris DeMarco noting that she’s “special” in her feel for the game. Perhaps most impressively, the Liberty have actually been better with Astier on the court (6.8 net rating) than with her on the bench (1.2 net rating), further underscoring just how important she’s been to a team with championship aspirations. Because of this, Astier will likely continue to be a key contributor for New York when the playoffs begin. DeMarco has been judicious thus far in how much he’s played several of his team’s veterans, such as Rebekah Gardner and Rebecca Allen, but with such a capable rookie having already proven herself in Astier, he may choose to continue to ride the hot hand.
